name: Umar Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do night trunks for a parcel company. I pick up a loaded trailer at the big sorting hub around ten at night, run it to one of three delivery depots, swap it, and bring the empties back, usually three runs before six in the morning. I like the quiet and the podcasts, and I like being trusted with a whole night's parcels. What wears me out is the sleep, because I never quite get it right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it, and how do you get through the nights?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just under two years, so I'm still the junior, still nervous on the tight depot gates. I use AI for everything: I ask a chatbot to plan my naps, I use it to revise for my class 1 theory, and it does our household budget. My girlfriend Leila is a freelance illustrator, and between us we've got about four months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, actually. I use these tools every day and I thought they'd do more. Online I'd probably post that the hype was mostly about selling shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask a chatbot to plan my naps between trunk runs, and that's about as far as the AI revolution has got in my cab. So my job is fine and Leila's work probably picks back up. In this picture, the parcel volumes matter more than AI, and they keep growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing nights and sit my class 1 test in the spring, so I can drive the bigger trailers for more money. I'd keep using AI for revision and budgets. And I'd put a bit aside for a deposit with Leila.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Leila's work picks back up. Has it been down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, she lost a few small jobs this year to people using image tools. Book covers, mostly. In this picture I think clients come back to her because the AI stuff looks samey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan for the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd like a small flat near the hub, so I'm not driving forty minutes home tired. We'd put 300 a month in together. It's slow, but it's a plan.

say: I'd say I'm a bit **disappointed**; I hoped the tools would do more.
I'd post that the **hype** was mostly about selling shares.
think: My job's **fine**, because parcel volumes keep growing in this picture.
I expect my girlfriend's **illustration work** to pick back up as clients tire of samey images.
do: Sit my **class 1 test** in spring to drive bigger trailers.
Keep using AI for **revision** and household budgets.
Put **300 a month** towards a flat near the hub with Leila.
S0.quote: I ask a chatbot to plan my naps between trunk runs, and that's about as far as the AI revolution has got in my cab.
fieldNote: Umar is an **everyday AI user** who is unimpressed when it stalls.
His household's soft spot is his girlfriend's **freelance income**, already dented this year.
He links a future flat to **tiredness** on the drive home.

steps.text: Sit the class 1 driving test in spring
Put 300 a month with Leila towards a flat near the hub

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a share of what these tools save, and the unions should be pushing for it. I'd post about Leila's industry, because illustrators are getting hit and nobody talks about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Leila draws for a living, and the AI already takes her small jobs, so in our flat the robots arrived through her laptop, not my truck. My driving is fine for years. But if her income halves, our deposit plan is gone and we're living on one night-shift wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hub manager about the new planning software and offer to help test it, because the people who understand it get kept. I'd do my class 1 and take extra nights for the money. Leila and I would cut back, probably eating out once a month instead of every weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mainly for her. I'm fine, we're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not her fault and it's not her drawing. Then I'd probably try to help her use the tools for the boring bits, which she'd hate. She's more stubborn than me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides what the household can afford if her income drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and a spreadsheet, honestly, and the chatbot that builds it. We'd sit down on a Sunday and cut. Rent first, then food, then everything else.

say: I'd say workers need a **share of savings** from AI, and unions should push.
I'd post about **illustrators** getting hit, because nobody talks about them.
think: My driving is safe for years, but my girlfriend's **income** could halve.
If that happens, the **deposit plan** is gone and we live on one wage.
do: Offer to **test** the hub's new planning software, so I'm kept.
Take **extra night shifts** after the class 1 test.
Cut eating out to **once a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for my girlfriend; I'm fine but the household isn't.
S1.quote: My girlfriend Leila draws for a living, and the AI already takes her small jobs, so in our flat the robots arrived through her laptop, not my truck.
fieldNote: The threat for Umar arrives through his **partner's work**, not his own.
He moves first: volunteering to **test software** to stay valued.
Household budgeting runs through **AI tools**, which he uses without irony.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the hub's new planning software
Take extra night trunk shifts once class 1 is passed
Cut eating out to once a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income, now, and I'd mean it. I'd share everything I could about it online. At the hub I'd tell people to join the union, even the agency lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI comes first, then the remote control rooms I wanted to work in are the first to go. Leila's work goes in 2028, and my truck goes around 2031. I'd be 31 with both of us out, and I'd have spent my best years learning things that died.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning a career in logistics offices straight away. I'd use the three years before the robots to drive every extra night going and save as much as possible. And I'd look for a hands-on trade that robots reach last, maybe fitting heat pumps, and start an evening course in year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window to earn. The truck is safe until about 2031, so I'd treat it as three years of overtime money. But that's also three years of watching the clock on my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does it feel different now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, weird. I'd still use it, because not using it would just make me slower. But it'd feel like asking the guy who's taking your job to help you write your CV.

say: I'd say we need a **basic income** now, and I'd mean it.
I'd tell everyone at the hub, even **agency drivers**, to join the union.
think: The **remote control rooms** I hoped to work in would go first.
My girlfriend's work goes in 2028 and my **truck** around 2031.
do: Drop plans for a **logistics office** career straight away.
Drive every **extra night** for three years and save hard.
Start an evening **heat pump** fitting course in year one.
feel: **Alarmed**; my stomach drops saying it out loud.
S2.quote: If thinking AI comes first, then the remote control rooms I wanted to work in are the first to go.
fieldNote: Umar sees the **thinking-first order** wiping out his planned next step.
He treats the truck's three remaining years as an **overtime window**.
His daily AI habit continues, but with a new sense of **betrayal**.

steps.text: Drive every extra night run for three years
Start an evening heat pump fitting course in the first year
Campaign for a basic income online and at the hub

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if we start now, and I'd say it to anyone in a union meeting. I'd share guides on how drivers can retrain. Online I'd be less angry and more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to get my class 1, save a deposit and learn a trade with my hands, in that order. Robots around 2034 means I've got eight years of driving. Leila's the one who needs a plan sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass my class 1 this year and switch to the bigger night trunks. In year two I'd start a part-time heat pump course. I'd help Leila find work teaching illustration at the college, because teaching feels safer than doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. Like having a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Leila needs a plan sooner. Does she agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. She thinks people will always want hand-drawn stuff, and maybe some will. I'd keep nudging her, and she'd keep telling me to stop nudging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out, mostly, and probably my old car. We'd also put off getting a dog, which sounds small but it's a big deal in our flat.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we start now.
I'd share **retraining guides** for drivers, more practical than angry.
think: Five years lets me get **class 1**, save a deposit and learn a trade.
My girlfriend needs a **plan sooner** than I do.
do: Pass the **class 1** this year and move to bigger night trunks.
Start a part-time **heat pump** course in year two.
Help Leila look for **teaching** work at the college.
feel: **Anxious** but organised, like having a to-do list.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get my class 1, save a deposit and learn a trade with my hands, in that order.
fieldNote: Umar turns the five-year warning into a clear **sequence of steps**.
There's quiet tension with his girlfriend over **how fast** to adapt.
Putting off **a dog** shows how planning reaches into home life.

steps.text: Pass class 1 and move to bigger night trunks this year
Start a part-time heat pump course in year two
Help Leila apply for illustration teaching at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be stupid. I'd push the union and the government to set up proper retraining schemes now. Online I'd be the annoying guy posting plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets me be early instead of desperate, and early is the only advantage someone like me ever gets. Robots come around 2039, when I'm 40. By then I want to be fitting or fixing things, maybe running a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive and save for the first few years, then train as a heat pump fitter by 2030. I'd start doing small jobs on weekends to build a name. I'd keep using AI for quotes and bookings, because that's the thinking part I can hand off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Hopeful, but it's still a big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work still arrive in 2039. Doesn't that catch the fitting trade too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably, eventually. But houses are messy and old, and I reckon fitting in a cramped loft is one of the last things robots do well. And by then I'd have savings and maybe a business to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leila do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to move into teaching or something new. We might even have a kid by then. Ten years means we can plan like normal people, not panic.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and wasting it would be stupid.
I'd push for proper **retraining schemes** to start now.
think: A decade lets me be **early** instead of desperate.
By **2039** I want to be fitting or fixing things, maybe in my own business.
do: Drive and save, then train as a **heat pump fitter** by 2030.
Do **weekend jobs** to build a name.
Use AI for **quotes and bookings** in the new work.
feel: **Uneasy**, hopeful but aware it's still a big change.
S4.quote: A decade lets me be early instead of desperate, and early is the only advantage someone like me ever gets.
fieldNote: Umar sees **being early** as his main edge, given little money.
He admits robots may reach fitting too, but bets on **messy old houses**.
Having **a child** returns to the conversation only in this slowest picture.

steps.text: Train as a heat pump fitter by 2030
Take weekend fitting jobs to build a name
Use AI tools for quotes and bookings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Leila and I would both lose work within three years of each other, and the job I'd planned to move into goes first. What would help is a basic income, or at least paid retraining, so I could learn a hands-on trade without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how people like me feel about the tools themselves. I'm the driver at the depot who talks to a phone all night, and I'm still not sure my phone is on my side.

headlineQuote: I'm the driver at the depot who talks to a phone all night, and I'm still not sure my phone is on my side.
portrait: Umar Mensah, 27, drives **night parcel trunks** and uses AI every day for naps, revision and budgets.
His household's weak spot is his girlfriend Leila's **illustration income**, already dented by image tools.
In the fast picture he sees his planned **office career** vanish first and pivots to a hands-on trade.
With a decade he plans heat pump **fitting** and feels being early is his only advantage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and his girlfriend would lose work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining, so he could learn a trade without losing the flat.
